rock-and-roll.note: A debut built around his Sun Studio sessions, announcing the birth of "rock and roll" by bridging R&B and country.
The album that single-handedly built the guitar vocabulary of rock and roll, epitomized by the riff of "Johnny B. Goode."
A debut that captured rock and roll's frenzied energy through shrieking vocals and breakneck piano.
Already establishing the self-contained singer-songwriter, this record set the template for the rock band lineup to come.

folk-rock.note: A transitional record where acoustic and electric coexist, shocking the folk scene and opening the door to folk rock.
A debut that rebuilt Dylan's songs with shimmering 12-string arpeggios, cementing "folk rock" as a genre name.
The high point of folk rock's aesthetic, perfecting delicate harmonies and orchestration.
The culmination of a rock trilogy made with Nashville session musicians, crystallizing poetic lyrics and band sound at the highest level.

surf-garage-rock.note: A landmark that moved past surf music's sunny image to open up the possibilities of the "album" through intricate arrangements and introspective lyrics.
An early landmark that converted West Coast surf culture and hot-rod pleasure directly into pop songs.
Produced by Andy Warhol, this record presented a prototype for garage/art rock through lyrics about drugs and transgression paired with experimental noise.
A singles-driven debut with a memorable organ riff that distills garage rock's raw impulse.

psychedelic-rock.note: A debut that condenses the dark, ritualistic worldview symbolized by "The End" and Jim Morrison's charisma.
A revolutionary debut that redefined what the guitar itself could do, stretching blues into psychedelia.
An album symbolizing San Francisco's counterculture, including "White Rabbit."
A classic that retains psychedelic improvisation while moving toward folk/country lyricism.

southern-rock.note: A live album capturing the interplay of twin guitars and extended improvisation — a landmark that perfectly captures the groove at the heart of southern rock.
The debut featuring "Free Bird," combining gritty guitar work with lyrics full of Southern pride.
An early ZZ Top landmark pairing distinctly Texan blues feel with humor.
An ambitious release combining studio and live recordings, issued after Duane Allman's sudden death.

arena-hard-rock.note: An early Aerosmith landmark balancing blues rock feel with American hedonism.
A live album that captured their flashy makeup and performance in sound alone — a record that conveys the excitement of arena rock.
A debut whose thick, polished guitar sound set the production standard for arena rock.
A landmark of shock rock, fusing horror theatrics with catchy rock songs.
A debut combining Eddie Van Halen's revolutionary guitar playing with hedonistic rock and roll.

proto-punk.note: Iggy Pop's impulsive performance and stripped-down guitar sound — a record that symbolizes the eve of punk rock's birth.
A live album recorded at a Detroit club, swirling with political radicalism and explosive playing.
A debut fusing cross-dressing glam excess with raw rock and roll, leaving a direct influence on the punk that followed.

punk-rock.note: A debut built from songs almost all under two minutes, stripped of ornamentation — this shaped the template for American punk.
An intellectual, defining work of the CBGB scene, fusing spoken-word poetry with rock and roll.
A singular record that retains punk's impulse while deploying intricate guitar interplay — a landmark of art punk.
A defining debut combining West Coast punk's ferocity with satirical politics.

new-wave.note: A record that boldly incorporated Afrobeat elements, developing new wave into more experimental, exhilarating dance music.
A landmark that fused punk energy, pop songcraft, and disco beats, and found commercial success as well.
A debut where nervy, angular funk coexists with pop songs, opening up new wave's more intellectual side.
A polished American new wave debut fusing power pop with synthesizers.

hardcore-punk.note: Their first album after Henry Rollins joined. Its raw, heavy guitar set the standard for hardcore punk.
The complete recordings of the Washington D.C. band that birthed straight edge culture — short, sharp songs distilling hardcore's aesthetic.
A debut of astonishing musicianship, careening at high speed between reggae and hardcore punk.
An ambitious double album that retains hardcore's velocity while boldly incorporating melody and experimentation.

college-rock-indie.note: A debut that established college rock's aesthetic through mumbled vocals and shimmering jangly guitar.
A record whose extreme loud/quiet dynamic shift had a massive influence on 1990s alternative rock.
A landmark double album of noise rock that wields alternate tunings and noise while still holding onto pop moments.
A key 1980s American indie record combining punk's rawness with power-pop songcraft.

glam-metal.note: A record distilling the hedonism and danger of the Sunset Strip, symbolic of the hair metal movement.
A debut balancing the rawness of the Los Angeles streets with pop melodies, marking the peak of the hair metal era.
A glam metal-era landmark that boldly embraces synthesizers while never losing its overwhelming guitar presence.

glam-metal.album: Look What the Cat Dragged In
glam-metal.note: A debut symbolizing hair metal's commercial peak with flashy makeup and catchy choruses.

heavy-metal.note: A record widely regarded as a landmark of thrash metal, balancing intricate song structures with overwhelming speed.
A record demonstrating thrash metal's technical peak through virtuosic twin-guitar work and intricate arrangements.
29 minutes of overwhelming speed and violence — an extreme landmark that also influenced the birth of death metal.
A heavyweight record that shaped the template for groove metal, combining aggression with a tight rhythmic pocket.

grunge.note: A historic record that pushed grunge into the mainstream, featuring "Smells Like Teen Spirit."
Pearl Jam's debut, fusing arena rock scale with grunge introspection.
A landmark that fused heavy-metal weight with psychedelic elements, showing off grunge's musical range.
One of grunge's most shadowed, affecting records, portraying addiction through heavy, dark sound.

alternative-rock.note: The record where the funk-rock band's personality bloomed most richly, including its more introspective songs.
A melodic alternative rock landmark, Dave Grohl's first serious effort as a full band after Nirvana's end.
A record that marked one of the peaks of 1990s alternative rock through thick, layered guitar sound and sweeping song structures.
A beloved 1990s alternative record combining power-pop accessibility with nerdy introspection.

pop-punk-emo.note: A record that channeled hardcore punk's velocity into pop melody, pushing pop-punk into a worldwide genre.
A landmark of 2000s emo, balancing concept-album architecture with emo's emotional intensity.
A major work depicting political anger through the format of a punk-rock opera, cementing the band's comeback.
A key record fusing emo's introspection with power-pop's uplift, bridging emo into the mainstream.

garage-indie-revival.note: A record that rebuilt the rawness of '60s garage rock through New York urban sensibility, becoming the starting point of the 2000s rock revival.
A record that draws out the primal power of blues and garage rock to its fullest with just guitar and drums.
The breakthrough record that led the garage rock revival's momentum through lo-fi production and impulsive playing.
A debut from a Southern band carrying on the southern rock lineage while playing with raw garage rock impulse.

other.note: A record that could be called the pinnacle of studio craft, translating advanced jazz vocabulary into a rock/pop context.
A defining roots-rock masterpiece of the 2000s, fusing Americana vocabulary with experimental sound processing.
A quintessential American rock album balancing country-rock lyricism with arena-rock scale.
Tom Petty's defining record, combining roots rock's solid craft with power-pop songcraft.
